title: ʻOkina & Kahakō
description: Train accurate Hawaiian spelling through noticing, handwriting, and recall after the word is hidden.

contentReview.standard: Spellings and basic meanings are checked against University of Hawaiʻi resources and Nā Puke Wehewehe before release.

activities.explanation: ʻAʻole has two ʻokina: one at the beginning and one between A and o. It does not use a kahakō.

activities.instruction: Study the word, then hide it and write it from memory.
activities.support: Notice exactly where each ʻokina appears before you hide the word.
studyNotes: Two ʻokina: one at the beginning and one between A and o
Say the word aloud while you study it

activities.explanation: You recalled the spelling after the word disappeared instead of copying it while it was visible.
Hawaiʻi has an ʻokina before the final i. The ʻokina is part of the spelling.

activities.instruction: Study the word, then hide it and write it from memory.
activities.prompt: Pay attention to exactly where the ʻokina occurs.

activities.explanation: The goal is to remember where the ʻokina belongs, not simply recognize it when it is shown.

activities.explanation: ʻŌlelo begins with an ʻokina and Ō has a kahakō. Hawaiʻi has an ʻokina before the final i.

activities.support: Notice the opening ʻokina, the kahakō over Ō, and the ʻokina in Hawaiʻi.
studyNotes: The Ō in ʻŌlelo has a kahakō
Hawaiʻi has an ʻokina before the final i

Write the spelling that means land or earth.
activities.support: Restore the ʻokina and kahakō for ʻāina.
activities.explanation: ʻĀina means land or earth. It begins with an ʻokina and the a carries a kahakō.

activities.instruction: Study the word, then hide it and write it from memory.
activities.prompt: This word means land or earth.
activities.support: Notice both marks before you hide the word.
studyNotes: The marks distinguish this spelling from other Hawaiian forms
activities.paperInstruction: Write the word you just studied three times on paper from memory. Say it aloud each time.
activities.explanation: The spelling of ʻāina includes both an initial ʻokina and ā.

activities.support: For the word meaning male or husband, restore the missing kahakō.
activities.explanation: Kāne uses a kahakō over the a.

activities.instruction: Study the word, then hide it and write it from memory.
activities.prompt: Remember where the long vowel is.
studyNotes: The dictionary includes male and husband among its meanings

activities.explanation: Mālama begins with mā. The Pukui-Elbert entry includes meanings such as take care of, tend, preserve, and protect.

activities.instruction: Study the word, then hide it and write it from memory.
activities.support: The kahakō belongs on the first a.
activities.paperInstruction: Write the word three times from memory. Underline the ā each time.
activities.explanation: Mālama has a kahakō on the first a.

activities.support: Restore the missing ʻokina and kahakō.
activities.explanation: ʻŌlelo begins with an ʻokina and ō. Pukui-Elbert includes language, speech, word, speak, and say among its meanings.

activities.explanation: ʻŌlelo is written with an initial ʻokina and ō.
